about: Facts for the chip diagram's second version (27 September 2026), read from the repository's data files.

facts.statement: The link trained at 16.0 GT/s x8 on all three cards in every run (sysfs current_link_speed and current_link_width): PCIe Gen4 x8, 15.75 GB/s per direction after 128b/130b coding.

Host to device, DMA only (the runtime's host-side copy replaced by a no-op, the analogue of pinned memory), 256 MB per copy: 12.47 [12.39, 12.55] GB/s on aifoundry2, 12.60 [12.55, 12.65] GB/s on aifoundry3, 12.46 [12.41, 12.50] GB/s on aifoundry1-c1 (mean of 5 runs [99% interval]): 12.46-12.60 GB/s, 79-80% of the link's 15.75 GB/s.

Device to host, DMA only, 256 MB per copy: 10.54 [10.43, 10.64] GB/s on aifoundry2, 10.41 [10.30, 10.52] GB/s on aifoundry3, 10.41 [10.38, 10.45] GB/s on aifoundry1-c1: 10.41-10.54 GB/s, 66-67% of the link figure, slower than host to device. The fastest device-to-host size is 16 MB on aifoundry2 (11.75 GB/s), 16 MB on aifoundry3 (10.99 GB/s), 16 MB on aifoundry1-c1 (10.69 GB/s).
facts.source: docs/reports/data/2026-09-27-pcie/pcie.json: bw.<card>.d2h.dma[bytes=268435456].gbs; the size of the largest bw.<card>.d2h.dma[].gbs.mean

facts.statement: The path a program takes, the runtime's staged copy (a host memcpy into a CMA bounce buffer, then the DMA), 256 MB: host to device 7.15 / 5.20 / 7.79 GB/s (5.20-7.79), device to host 6.53 / 4.78 / 6.97 GB/s (aifoundry2 / aifoundry3 / aifoundry1-c1). The hosts' own memcpy runs at 17.4 / 9.2 / 21.4 GB/s, and each staged rate is 98-100% of 1/(1/DMA + 1/memcpy): the runtime copies and then transfers, one after the other, so a slow host memcpy (aifoundry3's) cuts the staged rate on the same link to 0.67-0.73 of the other hosts' (host to device).

A DMA-only host-to-device copy reaches half its 256 MB rate at 2.0 / 2.1 / 2.2 MB per copy (aifoundry2 / aifoundry3 / aifoundry1-c1; n½, from the mean over five runs of log2 of the size): smaller copies are dominated by the per-command time.

A 4 KB copy issued after a random 0-1 ms gap takes 377 / 379 / 411 µs on average (377-411 µs; aifoundry2 / aifoundry3 / aifoundry1-c1; the mean over the four copy variants), while 200 queued 4 KB copies take 38 / 13 / 30 µs each (host to device, staged) and a wait on an idle stream 2.6 / 0.4 / 2.3 µs. The time of a lone small copy is the runtime's response polling, not the link.
The runtime's response thread polls the device's completion queue, sleeping 50 µs between polls while commands are in flight and 500 µs when none are.
facts.note: aifoundry3 runs a patched libetrt.so and aifoundry1 a fork build, so their constants may differ (PREREG.md).

facts.statement: An empty kernel on all 32 compute shires, launched and waited for: 566 / 556 / 565 µs (556-566 µs) from launch to completion (aifoundry2 / aifoundry3 / aifoundry1-c1); 100 launches queued back to back: 103.6 / 103.7 / 104.1 µs each (103.6-104.1 µs) on 32 shires and 91.2 / 92.2 / 92.4 on one shire. The card's own cost is the queued figure: a lone launch waited for adds 463 / 452 / 461 µs (452-463 µs, each run's difference), most of the runtime's 500 µs idle poll (fact pcie.poll), and a one-shire lone launch takes the same 566 / 556 / 565 µs.
facts.source: docs/reports/data/2026-09-27-pcie/pcie.json: launch.<card>.single_us."32".mean, launch.<card>.b2b_us."32".mean, .b2b_us."1".mean, .single_us."1".mean; predictions[id=P9b].per_card.<card>.value.mean (launch to completion minus back-to-back, per run)

facts.statement: Two host-to-device commands in flight on one stream move 6.09 / 6.09 / 6.03 GB/s (aifoundry2 / aifoundry3 / aifoundry1-c1), half the 12.39 / 12.48 / 12.28 GB/s of one command at a time (two streams: 5.96 / 6.00 / 5.96 GB/s in total); both directions at once, one command each at a time, move 16.97 / 16.89 / 16.92 GB/s together (2 × 64 MB per stream, DMA only).
facts.source: docs/reports/data/2026-09-27-pcie/pcie.json: conc.<card>.dma.h2d.agg_gbs.mean (no barrier: both commands of the stream in flight), ."h2d/ser" (a barrier on every copy), ."2xh2d", ."h2d+d2h/ser"

facts.statement: Renamed as the boot firmware renames the shires (NOC_Remap_Shires with its 'No displacement' table, used when no shire is fused off), the firmware's 'default Shire Virtual ID Map, based on the NOC spec' matches the measured map: 496 of 496 pair distances and 32 of 32 cells, with no rotation or mirror. As written, before the renaming, only 111 of 496 pair distances agree (fact L37).

In the firmware's maps the four cells that hold no compute shire are: logical (0, 3), shire 32, the master; (5, 3), shire 33, the spare; (0, 4), the PCIe shire ('pcie0' in the bridge map); and (0, 5), the I/O shire ('io0'). On this die view that puts the master in the north cell and the spare in the south one, with PCIe then I/O east of the master.
facts.note: To confirm on the cards: time a counter read on shire 32 from each compute shire (the hub's rung exp-mesh-stops).

facts.statement: The firmware's map puts memory shires mc0-mc3 at logical rows 1-4 on the west (y = -1) and mc4-mc7 at rows 1-4 on the east (y = 6): the DRAM-latency fit's places for the 7 memory shires the fit places on its own, provided the firmware's mcN is the memory shire that PA[8:6] = N selects. With those 7 in place, memory shire 2 has one cell left in the firmware's map as in the fit (fact ms2-forced): the map confirms the frame, not memory shire 2's place independently.
facts.note: Timing a counter read on each memory shire from every compute shire (the hub's rung exp-mesh-stops) would place memory shire 2 directly.

facts.statement: The die view follows the firmware's NoC-spec drawing and the Programmer's Reference Manual's Fig. 1-3: memory shires 0-3 on the west, PCIe then I/O at the east end of the top row. The published die plot draws I/O then PCIe, its mirror image; no document in the open drop says which handedness the silicon has.
facts.source: docs/reports/data/2026-09-27-chip-diagram/research/firmware_map.json; fact L24 (PRM Fig. 1-3 against the die plot)

facts.statement: An L3 read from another shire enters the home shire's cache through its L3 slave port and moves down the pipeline as L3_Read and L3_Fill: a miss goes out the to_sys mesh port to memory, the data comes back as the L3 fill, and the home answers the requester. The order memory shire, L3 home, requester is the specification's; which way each leg turns on the mesh is not documented.
facts.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf, pdf p.55 (§3.2.2 'L3 REQ_Read': 'They are received from the L3_slave and move down the pipeline as L3_Read and L3_Fill. Misses and victims are directed to the to_sys mesh port.', Figure 14)

facts.statement: One minion's TensorLoad of 16 lines (1 KB) into its L1 scratchpad: 160.4 cycles from the L2 and 160.1 from the own scratchpad, on all three cards; 4 lines from the L2 take 41.9 cycles. From DRAM, 16 lines take 748-751 cycles on passes 2 and 3 and 1,132-1,133 on the first pass.

All 1,024 minions tensor-loading at once: 256.0 cycles per 16-line load from the L2, and 7,994-8,037 cycles from DRAM (aifoundry2 / aifoundry3 / aifoundry1-c1: 8,037 / 7,994 / 8,021), where the memory shires set the pace.
A 16×16×16 fp32 TensorFMA with B streamed through TenB instead of held in the L1 scratchpad: 529.05-529.09 cycles on all three cards (A in the L1 scratchpad).

The matmul benchmark loads a new A (16 lines from the shire's L2 into one of two L1-scratchpad buffers) and streams B through TenB before every TensorFMA, issuing the next op's loads while the current FMA runs, and it takes 529.001 cycles per op on all three cards: no more than the TensorFMA alone with B through TenB (529.05-529.09 cycles), so the next A's load of about 160 cycles is hidden behind the FMA.
facts.note: A version that waits for each load before its FMA was never run; 160 + 529 cycles for it would be a derived figure, not a measured one.

facts.statement: The same benchmark with 64 private tiles per minion, so that every load comes from DRAM: 15,042-15,663 cycles per op and 0.309-0.312 TFLOP/s on the three cards, about 30 times slower than with the tiles in the L2.

The Horace runs of the fp32 matmul, 9.18 TFLOP/s on every data set (timed from the host over the whole run, its launches included), launched at 80.6-81.0 °C on aifoundry2: 38.29 W on zeros, 46.73 W on ones and 63.40 W on random data, the board's power at the launch temperature: its reading in seconds 1-3 of the run (38.29, 47.56 and 65.80 W) less the leakage that the run's own heating had added by then, at the fitted leakage slope. Idle before each run: 36.3 W.
facts.unit: W at the launch temperature (random data)
facts.source: docs/reports/data/2026-09-21-horace-aifoundry2/horace3.json: patterns.<zeros|ones|randn>.p80, .p_early, .p_before, .tflops, .start_temp; tools/ettelem/analyze_horace_strict.py:105-116 (tflops over t_start of the first launch to t_end of the last), :141 and :275 (p80 = p_early - leak x (t_early - launch temperature))
facts.note: Leakage-corrected, not a raw board reading: the raw mean board power over the random-data runs was 66.73 W.

facts.statement: The same matmul on the three cards (ABL-T8, watts above zeros at the board): ones 8.52 [7.70, 9.34], 8.09 [7.33, 8.86], 9.00 [7.33, 10.66] W and random data 25.33 [24.49, 26.17], 23.91 [23.51, 24.30], 26.66 [24.85, 28.48] W (aifoundry2 / aifoundry3 / aifoundry1-c1; 99% intervals): ones cost 8.1-9.0 W more than zeros and random data 23.9-26.7 W more. The registered test passed on aifoundry2 and aifoundry3; aifoundry1-c1 is reported against aifoundry2's registered values.

From a launch at 80.9-81.7 °C to the firmware's 90 °C cap on aifoundry2, the same matmul on all 1,024 minions: random data 19.1-26.3 s (4 runs), ones 107.1-166.9 s (3 runs); zeros never reached the cap in 602 s (3 runs).
facts.source: docs/reports/data/2026-09-21-horace-aifoundry2/long.json: runs[] with minions = 1024 and values = randn, ones, zeros: .dur, .reason (cap: reached 90 °C; time: the run ended first), .t_before
facts.note: One card: the three-card version (E47) was registered and not run.

facts.statement: Random data on fewer minions, the same launch and cap on aifoundry2: 768 minions 35.4 s, 512 minions 84.1 s, 384 minions 118.9 s, 256 minions 276.3-314.9 s, 128 never (602 s).
facts.source: docs/reports/data/2026-09-21-horace-aifoundry2/long.json: runs[] with values = randn and minions = 768, 512, 384, 256, 128: .dur, .reason

facts.statement: At 80 °C the card's idle power rises 0.65 W per °C (the fitted leakage law's slope, aifoundry2): a hotter die leaks more, which heats it further.

All 32 shires hammering one global atomic homed in shire 0 (32 minions each): every shire gets an even share, the host shire 1.004 / 1.004 / 1.004 of it (1.004) and the lowest 0.998 / 0.998 / 0.999 (0.998-0.999; aifoundry2 / aifoundry3 / aifoundry1-c1), at 10.00 cycles per atomic.
facts.page: One hot line stops a shire

facts.statement: The host shire's minions read their own scratchpad while the same number of minions in one other shire hammer one scratchpad word in the host shire: with 21 of each the host keeps 95.6 / 95.7 / 95.6% of its rate alone (aifoundry2 / aifoundry3 / aifoundry1-c1, mean of 3 passes; 95.5-95.7% over every pass), and with 22, 23 or 24 it stops: 0.02% on every card. An uncontended remote atomic takes 216.2 / 216.3 / 216.6 cycles round trip.
facts.unit: % of the rate alone (21 requesters, aifoundry2)
facts.page: One hot line stops a shire

facts.statement: The allreduce benchmark's tree: at level h, a minion whose ID has bit h as its lowest set bit sends its partial sum to the minion with that bit cleared (TensorReduce), levels 0 to 9, and the result comes back down the same tree (TensorBroadcast). Levels 0-2 join a neighbourhood's 8 minions along the fast network's edges, levels 3-4 its 4 neighbourhoods, levels 5-9 the 32 shires, rooted at minion 0 of shire 0.
facts.source: workloads/nocbench/kernel/nocbench.c:279-288 (tree: TensorReduce for levels 0..top, TensorBroadcast back), :516-521 ('Minion m receives at levels below ctz(m) and sends at ctz(m); the root (m = 0) receives at every level'); fact neigh.fln-edges for the tree edges
